nodes.notes: 1) Classification: dense elementwise binary add, no reductions, contiguous fp16 tensors of shape (16,2048,2048) => 67108864 elements. 2) Math: out[i]=x[i]+y[i]; fully independent per element, flatten to 1D. 3) Layout: all contiguous fp16; read x,y once, write out once; no reuse. 4) Regimes: (a) small N -> launch overhead dominates; (b) medium -> occupancy/coalescing matters; (c) large N (our case, 64M elts) -> pure DRAM bandwidth bound — only knob is achieving peak bandwidth via vectorized 128-bit loads, good occupancy, and minimal launch overhead. 5) Knobs: BLOCK_SIZE (1024..8192), num_warps (4/8), num_stages, vectorization (load as .uint4 / multiple elements per thread), grid 1D vs 2D, masked tail handling, possibly torch.empty vs empty_like. 6) Skeleton: 1D grid, each program loads BLOCK contiguous elements of x and y, adds, stores, with mask on tail. 7) Families: F1=Single fused 1D vectorized kernel (best, fits trivially); F2=2D grid mapping by (batch, spatial) (no benefit, same bandwidth); F3=Multi-element-per-thread unrolled kernel for ILP. Full fusion is the natural baseline since the op is already a single elementwise. Best limiter: DRAM BW (~1.7TB/s); theoretical min latency ~ 402MB/1.7TB/s ≈ 0.24ms.

kernel_summary: Dense elementwise fp16 add of two contiguous tensors of shape (16,2048,2048) = 67,108,864 elements. The operation is trivially parallel with zero reuse and no reductions, so it is strictly DRAM-bandwidth bound on RTX5090 (~1.7TB/s class). Total traffic ≈ 402 MB (2 loads + 1 store, fp16), giving a theoretical lower bound around ~0.24 ms. The only meaningful optimization axes are: (a) ensuring fully coalesced, wide (128-bit) loads/stores, (b) choosing BLOCK_SIZE and num_warps that saturate memory bandwidth while maintaining high SM occupancy, and (c) minimizing launch and indexing overhead. Tensor cores are irrelevant. Correctness requires only matching x+y in fp16 with proper tail masking.
open_questions: What BLOCK_SIZE / num_warps combination empirically saturates RTX5090 GDDR7 bandwidth for fp16 elementwise ops?
Does Triton on this toolchain automatically emit 128-bit vectorized loads for contiguous fp16, or do we need explicit packing?
Is torch.compile's generated kernel already near peak bandwidth, leaving little headroom to beat it?
Does using torch.empty (uninitialized output) vs empty_like have any measurable effect at this size?
Should we use a 1D flat grid or a 2D grid mapped to (batch, spatial) for better SM scheduling on Blackwell?
Are there alignment guarantees on the input tensors that allow assuming N is divisible by a large vector width (here 64M is divisible by everything reasonable)?
What is the measured reference latency from torch.compile to set a realistic speedup target?
